I'm in my fifties, been farming these fields in Quzhou since I was a young man. Never went to school, but I know my land. I've got about 6 mu, and every year I grow winter wheat followed by summer maize on the whole lot. That's what my father did, that's what my neighbors do, and it puts food on the table. I don't mess with cotton — too much work, too risky with prices.

This autumn, I'll sow wheat again. I'll go to the seed shop and buy the improved wheat seed everyone uses — costs a bit more than saving my own, but the yield is better and I don't have to worry about disease. For fertilizer, I'll spread two 50-jin bags of compound fertilizer per mu before planting — the 18-22-5 kind the dealer sells. That's what I've always done. In spring, if the wheat looks yellow at jointing, I'll topdress with half a bag of urea per mu. Can't afford to skip fertilizer; a bad wheat year hurts worse than wasting a few yuan on extra nutrients. I'll irrigate three times: once before winter to help the seedlings, once at jointing in spring, and once at grain filling if it doesn't rain. For pests and weeds, I'll spray herbicide once after sowing and insecticide once when I see aphids — maybe twice if they're bad.

After wheat harvest in June, the window is tight — only a few days. I'll plant hybrid maize right away, no time for tillage. Everyone here does no-tillage for maize; you just drill the seed into the wheat stubble. I'll put down about one and a half bags of the 28-6-6 compound fertilizer per mu at planting. Maize needs water at the critical stages, so I'll irrigate twice — once at jointing and once at filling, if the weather stays dry. Herbicide and one insecticide spray should be enough. If all goes well, I expect about 450 kg per mu of wheat and 500 kg per mu of maize. Not the highest in the village, but steady.
